clue.text: Swede, say, about to join golf-club having no English

indicators.note: the club is said to be without something, so a letter is taken out of it

parts.note: a brassie is an old wooden golf club, the number two wood
CA, short for circa, means about

explanation.surface: A recipe or garden note: a swede joins a golf club that has dropped its English members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swede' looks like a person from Sweden, but it is the vegetable. Remove E from BRASSIE to get BRASSI, then CA goes on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The swede is a root vegetable of the cabbage genus, so it is an example of that plant family.

clue.text: Being British, swallowed rage

parts.note: to swallow food is to eat it, so swallowed is ate

explanation.surface: Being British, he swallowed his anger.
explanation.walkthrough: Bate is an old word for a fit of temper, still heard as 'in a bate'. 'Being' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Bate is British slang for a fit of anger, so it fits rage as a noun.

clue.text: One very skilful crosses mile high peak

indicators.note: the expert goes across the mile, so it ends up around it

parts.note: an ace is someone very skilful

explanation.surface: A skilled climber covers a mile to reach a high peak.
explanation.definitionFit: Acme means the highest point or summit, a figurative sense of a high peak.

clue.text: Taking lots of support for body in raid

indicators.note: in says the support goes inside the word for raid

parts.note: a sortie is a raid made out from a defended position
a leg supports the body

explanation.surface: Lots of support for the body's troops during a raid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking lots' means drawing lots, not taking plenty. 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Sortilege is divination by drawing lots, so it is the act of taking lots.

clue.text: Pioneer scout lost balance

indicators.note: lost means the letters have lost their way and come out in a new order

parts.note: the word as written
the word as written

explanation.surface: A pioneering scout loses his balance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost' rearranges the twelve letters of PIONEER SCOUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A counterpoise is a weight that balances another, so it is a synonym of balance as a noun.

clue.text: This extended farewell

definitions.meaning: read literally as '...' meaning this length, stretched out
a casual way of saying goodbye

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both a goodbye and, read literally, 'this long' describing something stretched to a length.

clue.text: Daggers plunged into centre of tapestry

indicators.note: only the centre of the word for tapestry is used, its first and last letters dropped

parts.note: a Gobelin is a tapestry from the famous Gobelins works in Paris

explanation.surface: Daggers thrust into the middle of a wall hanging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre of' strips G and N from GOBELIN. 'plunged into' is a link. Daggers are the printer's marks, not weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Obeli are the dagger symbols used in printing for footnotes, the plural of obelus.

clue.text: Prove awkward to lift, being flatter

indicators.note: awkward signals the word beside it is set out awkwardly, in a new order

parts.note: the word as written
to lift is to raise

explanation.surface: Something proves awkward to lift, being flatter than expected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkward' rearranges PROVE to OVERP. 'to' and 'being' are links. 'flatter' looks like a comparative adjective, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To overpraise is to praise too much, which is what flattering someone means.

clue.text: Such a good view of Great Bear?

parts.note: grand means great
to bear is to stand, as in tolerate

explanation.surface: A question about the Great Bear constellation and the fine view of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great Bear' looks like the constellation, but it is two words for two pieces. 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandstand view is an idiom for an excellent view, as from the main stand at a sports ground.

clue.text: Nervous, drop back — finally failing to get going

indicators.note: back says the word for drop is read from right to left

parts.note: to drop something is to omit it

indicators.note: the last letter of the word for get going fails, dropping off the end

parts.note: to rouse is to stir someone up and get them going

explanation.surface: A nervous person keeps dropping back and, at the end, cannot get going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns OMIT into TIMO; 'finally failing' takes the last E off ROUSE, leaving ROUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Timorous is a synonym of nervous, describing someone timid and easily frightened.

clue.text: Types encountered in information age

parts.note: GEN is British slang for information
an era is an age or period

explanation.surface: Kinds of thing you come across in the information age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'encountered in' is a link here, not a container signal; GEN is everyday British slang for facts.
explanation.definitionFit: Genera, plural of genus, are classes or kinds, so types is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Colourful evidence of skill in bed?

definitions.text: Colourful evidence of skill in bed?

parts.words: Colourful evidence of skill in bed?
parts.note: a colour-named sign of talent in the flower bed, with bed hinting at the bedroom

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a British idiom for a natural talent for growing plants, as shown in a flower bed.

clue.text: Such a drag, expected to be winning on screen

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece on another means it comes after it

parts.note: a screen is a filter, something that sifts
a horse tipped to win is expected to be winning

explanation.surface: A tedious screen performance, by someone tipped to win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drag' looks like tedium, but it is a pull on a cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: A drag on a filter-tipped cigarette is an example of such a puff, so the clue defines by example.

clue.text: Grand pair of volumes

parts.note: piano means soft in music, one volume level
forte means loud in music, the other volume level

explanation.surface: A grand two-volume set of books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'volumes' look like books, but they are loudness levels.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand is a large concert piano, an example of the instrument named in full.

clue.text: Signs of expecting lunch — it's being delivered around one

indicators.note: around says the word for being delivered goes round the next piece

parts.note: salvation is being delivered from sin or danger
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Lunch is on its way, delivered around one o'clock, and mouths water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Salivation is the flow of saliva, the mouth-watering sign that a meal is anticipated.

clue.text: Furious buccaneer won't keep quiet

indicators.note: the pirate refuses to hold on to a letter, so it is dropped

parts.note: a buccaneer is a pirate
P, for piano, means quiet in music

explanation.surface: A pirate in a rage, unable to keep his voice down.
explanation.definitionFit: Irate is a synonym of furious, meaning very angry.

clue.text: Nothing salient seen about candidate

parts.note: RE means about or concerning
an entrant is a candidate in a contest

explanation.surface: Nothing remarkable has been seen about the candidate.
explanation.walkthrough: A salient angle points outwards; a re-entrant angle points inwards, so it is in no part salient. 'seen' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry and fortification a re-entrant angle is the opposite of a salient one, pointing inwards.

clue.text: Fungus stood a lot, when cooking

indicators.note: cooking signals the words are mixed up into something new

parts.note: the word as written
the word as written
the word as written

explanation.surface: A fungus stood about a lot while the cooking went on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A toadstool is a mushroom-like fungus, usually one thought poisonous.

clue.text: The sound of wings?

parts.note: wings here are the sides of a theatre stage, and the sound is what comes from offstage there

explanation.surface: The beating sound a bird's wings make.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a stage direction for sounds made offstage, that is, from the wings of the theatre.

clue.text: But it doesn't usually attract a light sentence

definitions.text: But it doesn't usually attract a light sentence

parts.words: But it doesn't usually attract a light sentence
parts.note: the crime of deliberately setting things alight usually draws a heavy prison term; light plays on lighting fires

explanation.surface: A remark about a crime that tends to bring a heavy sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting fire to property is a serious crime, so it rarely brings a lenient sentence, with light as fire.

clue.text: Perfect state's feeble head leads to anarchy

indicators.note: the head of feeble, its first letter, leads, going at the front

parts.note: anarchy is a state of lawlessness

explanation.surface: A political jibe: a weak leader takes the state into anarchy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' is not a leader here: 'head leads' takes the first letter of 'feeble' and puts it in front. 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Flawlessness is the condition of being without defect, which is the state of being perfect.

clue.text: City has scored first, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals the word is said, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a team that has scored first leads

explanation.surface: A football report: the City side has scored first.
explanation.walkthrough: Leeds is a city in Yorkshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeds is a large city in West Yorkshire, England, an example of a city.

clue.text: Set of papers used in biography oddly switched

indicators.note: the letters in odd positions, first and third, switch places

parts.note: a biography is a life, the word used in titles such as The Life of Johnson

explanation.surface: Papers used in a biography were oddly switched around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly switched' swaps the first and third letters of LIFE.
explanation.definitionFit: A file is a folder or collection of papers kept together, so set of papers fits.

clue.text: Wait to speak, having limited time

indicators.note: having means holding, so the word for speak holds the next piece

parts.note: to say is to speak
T, a cut-down form of time, is its abbreviation

explanation.surface: Waiting to speak with only limited time available.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay is to remain or wait where you are, a synonym of wait.

clue.text: Cavalryman perhaps captures a marauder

indicators.note: the rider takes the next letter prisoner, holding it inside

parts.note: a cavalryman is an example of a rider

explanation.surface: A mounted soldier catches a raider.
explanation.definitionFit: A raider is someone who makes plundering attacks, a synonym of marauder.

clue.text: Assume one's in the wrong to be pleasure-seeker

indicators.note: in says these pieces go inside the jumbled word
wrong signals the little word beside it is set out wrongly

parts.note: to don a garment is to assume it
one's stands for one is, giving I and IS read as a word

explanation.surface: Thinking yourself in the wrong makes you a seeker of pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges THE into HET; 'in' puts DONIS inside it to give HE-DONIS-T. 'to be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedonist pursues pleasure as the chief good in life, so a pleasure-seeker is a direct synonym.

clue.text: One way to avoid most serious man

indicators.note: the word for serious avoids, or leaves out, a letter

parts.note: earnest means intensely serious
an A-road is one kind of British main road, so A is one way

explanation.surface: Advice on how to steer clear of the most serious man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One way' is A, from Britain's A-roads, its main roads. Wilde's joke, Ernest versus earnest, sits behind the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernest is a man's first name, so the answer is an example of a man.

clue.text: Spy moving about without disguise, the plucky thing

indicators.note: without means outside, so the jumble goes around the next piece
the letters of the word spy move about into a new order

parts.note: the word as written
to disguise something is to alter it

explanation.surface: A spy goes about undisguised; brave of him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving about' scrambles the spy's letters to PSY; 'without' puts that outside the synonym for disguise. A psaltery is plucked, hence the pun on plucky.
explanation.definitionFit: A psaltery is an old stringed instrument played by plucking, hence a thing that is plucked.
